entries.text: Tung said the developer is the central early adopter for AI.
After two years Anthropic completed an IPO that raised $81.3 billion, giving a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion and a paper return of roughly 15 times for Notable’s stake.

Anthropic’s growth comes as enterprise customers increasingly prefer U.S.‑based, closed‑source models for mission‑critical tasks, a factor highlighted by Notable’s experience with U.S–China investment dynamics.
Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund GIC also entered Anthropic in 2025 after meeting CFO Krishna Rao, later leading larger rounds at $183 billion and $380 billion valuations.
These moves illustrate how venture capital is betting on a narrow set of large AI labs despite market volatility.

OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published a blog post proposing perplexity as a metric to limit AI development speed.
The idea follows recent calls from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to set common safety standards and pace the frontier.
Pachocki argues that a shared benchmark could help companies agree not to exceed a defined threshold until monitoring capabilities improve.
Pachocki notes that downstream capability benchmarks become outdated quickly, while perplexity—measuring how well a model predicts the next token—remains informative.

He cites a chart showing OpenAI model perplexity falling from GPT‑3.5 to GPT‑4, which sits at roughly 0.91, and newer models dropping below 0.8, coinciding with the emergence of capabilities in cybersecurity and mathematics.
The post suggests that once perplexity reaches a low enough value, companies could commit to a “speed limit” until they achieve concrete monitoring milestones.
Perplexity is a standard language‑model metric: lower values indicate more accurate token predictions.
Using it as a progress gauge differs from task‑specific benchmarks that quickly become obsolete as models improve.
The proposal aims to create a common, quantifiable target for AI safety agreements, echoing broader industry concerns about catastrophic or existential risks.

Wells Fargo is updating its customer agreement starting Tuesday to address AI agents.
The new terms state that using any AI agent is at the customer's own risk.
This move follows similar actions by other major US banks in late 2026.
JPMorgan Chase banned third-party agents that log in with user credentials in late October.
Bank of America warned customers not to share login info with agents on the same day.
Citibank and PNC have also updated their terms to include warnings about agents.
AI agents automate online tasks by clicking on a user's behalf.
While useful for shopping, they can make errors like posting private details.
Users often grant sweeping permissions without considering security risks, leading to friction with service providers.
